hero.h1: Electric car charging cable at home: Type 2, portable charger and what not to do
hero.lead: At home you use one of two cables: a portable charger that plugs into a wall socket or a Type 2 cable for a wallbox with a socket. Neither one is extended with an extension cord or plugged in through an adapter or splitter.

card.title: Electric car charging cable
card.text: Portable charger, Type 2 cable and Type 1: what you need at home and what you never do with a cable.

blocks.p: A charging cable is not an ordinary extension lead. Inside it or at its end there is electronics that agrees the current with the car and stops charging when something is wrong. That is why it matters which cable you use and where you plug it in.

p: Which cable you need depends on what you have on the wall: a socket or a wallbox. If that is not sorted yet, start with the page

blocks.h2: Two kinds of cable for charging at home

blocks.p: A portable charger has a household plug at one end, a control box in the middle and a car connector at the other end. You plug it into a wall socket. Some car makers include it with the car, for others you buy it separately.

A Type 2 cable has a Type 2 connector at both ends and no control box. One end goes into a wallbox with a Type 2 socket, the other into the car. You use the same cable at public AC chargers that have a socket instead of their own cable.

p: If your wallbox has a fixed cable, you do not need another cable at home. The differences between the two wallbox versions are covered in the guide

p.a: wallbox with a cable or a socket

blocks.h2: Portable charger: what the control box does

blocks.p: The control box has residual current protection and a current setting. For example, one portable charger for a household socket has 30 mA protection for AC and 6 mA for DC fault current. A temperature sensor in the connector reduces or stops charging when it gets too hot.

The same device charges at 16 A from the factory and has a lower 10 A mode that can go down to 6 A. The maker recommends the lower mode when the socket's fuse is weaker than the charger's current. Kia writes in its manual that if you do not know what the socket can take, you choose the lowest charging current.

At 10 A the charger gives about 2.3 kW. That is enough for shorter daily drives, but charging every day on an old socket is not a good solution. The maker of the same charger recommends having the charging installation checked by an electrician.

Some portable chargers have adapters for industrial CEE sockets, the red three-phase one and the blue single-phase one. Such a socket on its own circuit is installed by a licensed electrician. You use an adapter only in the socket the maker designed it for.

blocks.h2: Type 2 cable for a wallbox: current and number of phases

blocks.p: Since 2013 Type 2 has been the standard connector for AC charging in the European Union. It supports single-phase and three-phase charging. In common practice that is up to 7.2 kW on one phase and up to 22 kW on three phases.

Type 2 cables differ in the number of phases and in current rating. A resistor in the plug tells how much current the cable can carry, for example 13, 20, 32 or 63 A. The car stops charging if the current would go over that limit.

An 11 kW wallbox needs a three-phase cable rated for at least 16 A. A single-phase cable does not carry three phases, so a car with a three-phase on-board charger would charge more slowly on it. A cable rated for more current than your wallbox delivers does not speed up charging.

Buy a cable as long as you need to reach the car's inlet, with a little slack. The cable must not run across a walkway or someone else's parking spot. Tesla's manual for its portable charger asks that the cable not obstruct pedestrians or other vehicles.

blocks.h2: An older car with a Type 1 inlet

blocks.p: Type 1 is a single-phase charging connector used in North America and Japan. The first European versions of some models, for example the Nissan Leaf and Chevrolet Volt, had a Type 1 inlet before Type 2 became the standard.

For such a car at a wallbox with a Type 2 socket you use a cable with a Type 2 plug at one end and Type 1 at the other. Nissan supplied exactly that kind of cable. Since Type 1 is single-phase, the car charges over one phase even on a three-phase wallbox.

blocks.h2: What you never do with a cable

blocks.p: The manuals of portable charger and car makers say the same here:

ul: You do not use an extension cord, a splitter, an adapter or a power strip.
You do not plug the charger into a damaged, loose, worn or ungrounded socket.
You do not use a cable, plug or control box that is cracked, damaged or has exposed wires.
You do not pull the plug out of the wall socket while the car is charging.
You do not plug into a socket that is wet or covered in snow.
You do not step on the cable, drag it across the floor or kink it, and you never drive over it.

blocks.p: Two Type 2 cables cannot be joined into a longer one either. The standard prevents it on purpose: one pin on the plug is shorter, so a cable cannot serve as an extension.

If the cable does not reach the car, the solution is a charger closer to the spot, not a longer cable or a joint. The same goes for a socket in your apartment: a cable through the window or down the stairs to the parking lot is not a solution.

blocks.h2: How to look after the cable

blocks.p: After charging, coil the cable and do not leave it on the floor. Do not drop the control box or put heavy things on it. Kia writes in its manual that you do not wrap the cable around the box itself.

Look at the cable, the plugs and the socket regularly. If you see a crack in the insulation or a damaged plug, do not use the cable until a qualified person checks it. A damaged or worn socket is replaced by a licensed electrician.

p: If you use a portable charger every day, the socket should be on its own circuit and built for long loads. Evolako START is such a reinforced socket with a MID meter, 2.3–3.7 kW, and you can see all packages on the page
